question: A service manager wants to use Claude to improve a customer refund process that everyone agrees is too slow. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Map how the process actually runs today; have Claude propose where time is being lost; test those proposals against real cycle-time records; agree the changes with the people who run the steps.
B) Map how the process actually runs today; agree the changes with the people who run the steps; have Claude propose where time is being lost; test those proposals against real cycle-time records.
C) Test those proposals against real cycle-time records; have Claude propose where time is being lost; map how the process actually runs today; agree the changes with the people who run the steps.
D) Have Claude propose where time is being lost; map how the process actually runs today; agree the changes with the people who run the steps; test those proposals against real cycle-time records.
correct_answers: A) Map how the process actually runs today; have Claude propose where time is being lost; test those proposals against real cycle-time records; agree the changes with the people who run the steps.
explanations: Correct. The map grounds the analysis in the real process, Claude then does the pattern work of pointing at likely losses, the cycle-time records separate genuine bottlenecks from plausible-sounding ones, and the people who run the steps agree changes that have already been evidenced.
Agreeing changes immediately after mapping commits the team before Claude has identified anything, and the evidence check lands at the very end when the changes are already settled.
There are no proposals to test at the start, so the first step has nothing to act on, and mapping the process arrives after the analysis that depended on it.

Asking for proposals before the process is mapped means Claude reasons from an assumed refund process rather than this one, and the changes are agreed with the team before anyone has tested whether they hold.
